question: In the proof of the λ₂ upper bound for planar graphs, what property does the separator X have, and how is the bipartite subgraph's edge count used to bound λ₂ in Case 2 (the case where |E_C| exceeds (2 − K/8)n)?
expected_answer: By Lemma 3.1, G has a separator X of constant size such that each component of G − X has at most n/3 vertices; the subgraph (V, E_{X,G−X}) is bipartite and planar with at most 2n − 4 edges, giving λ₂ ≤ 2/(n − |X| − 4), which is 2 + O(1/n).

question: For the STORM stochastic trust region method, what expected complexity bound is established for reaching a first-order ε-stationary point, and how does it compare with the deterministic version of the algorithm?

expected_answer: It is unlikely that a closed-form efficient solution can be derived for it, so an approximation to the solution of Cp (the 'approximate Cp') is derived instead.

question: In the simulation where two BDI agents and an EMA agent estimate the center of a distribution from sampled observations, which of the BDI agents' trajectories of estimates behaves like a Lévy walk, and what power-law exponent describes its step-length distribution?

question: In the analysis of the energy-based A/C approximation, endpoint cases p ∈ {1, ∞} arise in both the Lipschitz estimate (5.4) for δE_a and the auxiliary estimate proved in Appendix A. How is each handled: how are the cases p = 1 and p = ∞ established for the Lipschitz bound (5.4), and how is the case p = ∞ obtained in the proof of the Appendix A estimate?

question: The cost bound for evaluating a regular reachability query qrr(s, t, R) on a fragmentation makes running time grow quadratically with the size of the regular constraint R. question: In this EPT-based guest-isolation design, execution rights are stripped from all guest pages and handed back only once the page is confirmed free of a 2.5-byte signature — yet the trusted driver's code pages are exempt from this treatment. Why must they be exempt, and how are they handled instead?
expected_answer: The driver's entry and exit points deliberately contain the 2.5-byte sequence — its two address-space-switching instructions run without VM exits and are the only legitimate occurrences in the guest's executable address space — so the absence check could never pass there; instead, the driver's pages are verified when the driver is loaded.

checks.note: Closed-book answer wrongly cites VMCALL 0F 01 C1 instead of mov-to-cr3 as the legitimate 2.5-byte sequence.

question: In the context of edge computing for connected low-power devices, why is performing medical image processing locally on the edge node more energy-efficient than sending the raw imaging data to a remote server for analysis?
expected_answer: Because image processing workloads are data-rich (memory/compute intensive and requiring large storage), and transmitting data consumes significantly more energy than computing on it locally—per the cited sensor node study, sending one bit takes 1500-2000X the energy of executing a single instruction.

question: In the CDC questionnaire study, prototypes were added for each questionnaire up to m = 10, beyond which the objective (eq. 3) improved only incrementally. What two termination criteria does the prototype selection algorithm support, and how do they correspond to these stopping behaviors?
expected_answer: It can stop at a sparsity level m, or at a minimal increase in objective value ε required for selecting more elements; the m = 10 choice reflects the former, and the incremental-improvement cutoff reflects the latter.

question: In the proposed in-storage PIM accelerator for Transformer inference, which computational tasks are executed on the dedicated PIM banks inside the memory subsystem, and where is the intermediate data that those tasks consume kept between Transformer blocks?
expected_answer: Attention and activation-function tasks run on the dedicated PIM banks in the DRAM subsystem, while the intermediate activation data between Transformer blocks is stored in the DRAM buffer.

question: In the multi-task brain MRI prediction framework with independent and sequential prediction channels, learned features from one task can help predict unrelated target tasks, so why was the sequential training limited to a task-sequence length of 6 rather than using longer sequences?
expected_answer: Because although cross-task knowledge transfer is real (features learned in many tasks are useful for unrelated tasks), longer sequences (9+) showed high validation performance but poor test generalization; length 6, statistically best after FDR correction, balances knowledge transfer benefits against noise accumulation and overfitting.

expected_answer: It matches benchmarking reports that results remain sensitive to evaluation protocol and fine-tuning strategy, and that larger pretrained models do not uniformly outperform smaller or task-specific alternatives — mirroring the stroke result where increased model capacity gave no adaptation gain.

question: In this study of LLM-based scoring of health and life science journal articles, why can the authors not determine whether the higher scores awarded when the model reads the entire article rather than just its title and abstract reflect genuine research quality?
expected_answer: Because no expert review scores exist as a gold standard, the extent of bias in the LLMs is unclear and it is not known whether one or both input approaches are biased; the higher scores may simply reflect models guessing that extensive methods details indicate good research when they cannot model complex methods.

question: In GLANCE's speculative decoding setup for vision-language models, how many drafting passes per round does GLANCE spend, and how many sequential drafting passes does the deployed drafter pay in the configuration where that drafter runs fastest?
expected_answer: GLANCE spends a single draft pass per round (it fills a whole block in one forward pass), while the deployed drafter pays eight passes a round at its fastest, so GLANCE saves seven per round.

question: In the NeoMME training recipe, the tiled late-interaction kernel (LIK) is adopted to cut scoring memory — does it also speed up training at the 260M model's training shape, and what mean latency does that same 260M variant record when encoding a single text query on an Apple M5 Pro?
expected_answer: No — throughput at the 260M training shape is within run-to-run variation, so LIK's benefit is memory headroom rather than speed; the 260M variant's mean latency for one text query on the Apple M5 Pro is 15.9 ms.

question: Across the 600-episode evaluation of two configurations that share the same arena, observation space, action space, base reward function, and PPO hyperparameters, to what does the study attribute the statistically significant performance differences observed against the three opponent bot types?
expected_answer: The presence or absence of LLM guidance — i.e., whether the strategy tag is selected at runtime by Mistral 7B rather than held at zero.

question: How can one decide whether a plane curve interpolation problem with a single general point of multiplicity 2^t over an infinite field of characteristic 2 is almost regular, and does the multiplicity 2^(t+1) case reduce to multiplicity 2^t cases?
expected_answer: Yes. For n = |Z| = 1 and m = 2^t the problem is completely solved in characteristic 2: the scheme ⟨S, T_{2^(t+1)}⟩ is almost regular iff no triple (U, V, W) drawn from the three restricted parts of S (Definition 2.3) exists, so almost regularity is inductive in t.

question: Can an unknown density be estimated from a single numerical data sequence without assuming the data come from a stationary stochastic process, and what kind of procedure does the paper propose for this setting?
expected_answer: Yes. The paper estimates an unknown density from an individual numerical sequence that need not be a trajectory of a stationary process, proposing a simple procedure applicable in a purely deterministic setting; such deterministic analyses can also apply to individual sample paths in a stochastic setting.

question: In the higher-order generalization of the Little model for associative memory, what symmetry conditions must the third-order connection strengths satisfy for an energy function to be defined?
expected_answer: The third-order couplings must be equal under all permutations of the indices when i, j, k are distinct, and must vanish whenever any of the indices coincide; analogous symmetry requirements apply to still higher-order connections.

question: In the clustering-based rounding for the uncapacitated location problem, after the scaling step gives each client more fractional connectivity than its demand r_j, how are the client's close and distant candidate sites separated, and why isn't the site that falls into both sets simply split between them?
expected_answer: Sites with positive x^(c) — enough scaled mass to cover rj — form the close set Cj; those with positive x^(d), the excess connectivity, form the distant set Dj. They overlap in at most one site, which cannot be split because the final integral solution must make at most one connection there.

checks.note: Closed-book gives a different rationale for not splitting than the at-most-one-connection reason in the excerpt.

question: In the call-by-need calculus, when proving that a program transformation is correct, why is it sufficient to test convergence only in S-contexts rather than quantifying over all contexts?
expected_answer: The context lemma says (S[s]⇓ ⇒ S[t]⇓) holds for every S-context S iff it holds for every context C, i.e. s ≤c t; since every R-context is also an S-context, checking S-contexts suffices.

question: What is the deeper connection between support vector machines and large margin nearest neighbor, beyond both using a margin and hinge loss — can one be formulated in terms of the other?
expected_answer: Yes: SVM can be formulated as a distance learning problem, and the nearest neighbor method can be seen as a set of local SVM-like classifiers in a quadratic space; it is actually even more similar to the proposed ε-SVM variant than to standard SVM.

checks.note: Closed-book describes a single linear SVM in M-space rather than a set of local SVM-like classifiers closer to ε-SVM.

question: For the graph class defined by excluding K_h as a minor, what upper bound is derived on the maximum possible second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue λ2 over n-vertex graphs, and how does it differ between h ≤ 9 and large h?
expected_answer: For h ≤ 9, λ2^max ≤ (h−2) plus a small error term, since such graphs have fewer than (h−2)n edges; for large h, λ2^max is at most αh log h plus error, with α = 0.319... + o(1).

question: In the parallel evaluation of a regular reachability query over a large graph, what bounds the input size at each stage of processing, and what is the overall ECC of the algorithm?
expected_answer: Each worker's input is bounded by O(|Fm|), where Fm is the largest fragment; the single collecting node's input is bounded by O(|R|^2|Vf|^2), where Vf is the set of nodes in the fragment graph; the overall ECC is O(|Fm| + |R|^2|Vf|^2).

question: In the computer algebra proof of identity (10.1.48), what substitution is used to get around the fact that sin(θ) is not algebraic?
expected_answer: They replace cos(θ) by the variable c and sin(θ) by √(1 − c²), which makes the identity accessible to the software.

question: Which causal discovery algorithm is provably able to identify the true Markov equivalence class under assumptions strictly weaker than the weakest previously known sufficient conditions, and what consistency guarantees (including under hypothesis testing errors) does it come with?
expected_answer: The SP algorithm. It is pointwise consistent, i.e., it recovers the correct Markov equivalence class when the distribution is Markov to the true graph, and the paper additionally derives uniform consistency guarantees that account for hypothesis testing errors.

question: How does rational reconstruction use the extended Euclidean algorithm to recover a rational number a/b from its image u under a large integer m, and what bound on m guarantees the reconstruction is unique?
expected_answer: Run the EEA on m and u; every step yields gi/ti matching a/b, and the special step j—the first gi with |gi| ≤ ⌊m/2⌋, where also |tj| ≤ ⌊m/2⌋ and GCD(tj, gj) = 1—gives gj/tj = a/b. Classically m must be greater than 2 max{a², b²}; the modern variant succeeds with high probability once m > 2|a||b|.

question: In the scheduling of quantum circuit operations across multiple quantum cores, how does the problem formulation differ from the analogous latency-driven scheduling problem in high-level synthesis that it resembles?
expected_answer: The high-level synthesis problem ignores the cost of moving data among resources, whereas here the quantum cores lie on a grid, so their average communication costs can be computed ahead of time.

question: When randomizing the order of system calls, why does the transformation only delay calls in the set S instead of every system call the program makes?
expected_answer: Because calls outside S generally read information that applications need in order to keep executing properly, so holding them back would break the program's functionality.

checks.note: Closed-book answer cites shared-state overhead instead of blocking needed reads.

question: What kind of operator maps one orthonormal basis of a system's Hilbert space to another, and does applying such an operator to a basis always yield a valid basis again?
expected_answer: A unitary operator. Applying a unitary to an ONB produces another ONB, and given any two ONBs there always exists a unitary operator mapping one basis to the other, and vice versa.

question: In a virtualized network I/O design where the NIC writes incoming packets directly into guest-provided buffers, how is a packet delivered when it lands in a buffer owned by a guest other than its destination?
expected_answer: The buffer cannot simply be handed to the destination guest since it does not own it; instead, a fresh buffer is allocated from the destination guest, the packet contents are copied into it, and the new buffer is passed to the destination guest's receive ring. Such mismatches also mean received buffers can arrive out of ring-allocation order.

checks.note: Closed-book answer describes page-ownership exchange, while excerpt specifies copy into fresh destination buffer.

question: In the GLM point-process model of call events between individuals, which smooth function replaced the strict max(0,·) link function, what scaling constant c was chosen for it, and why?
expected_answer: A smooth clipped-linear replacement was used because the strict max(0,·) form often failed in optimisation; c = 10 was chosen as large enough to closely approximate the hard clip without causing numerical optimisation problems.

question: In a distributed heterogeneous IoT network where devices have different types of compute cores, what costs must be weighed before offloading an application to a more capable node when the local node cannot meet its deadline?
expected_answer: The energy and time to transfer the application to the better-suited node, plus the time to retrieve the results, must not outweigh the savings from executing it on that node.

question: How can the effective dimensions of a point be expressed as pointwise dimensions of a measure, and what does that imply about the global dimensions of the measure constructed for this purpose?
expected_answer: For each oracle A ⊆ N, the section defines an outer measure κ^A on R^n via a minimum of K^A-complexity contributions over rational balls (infinite when E ∩ Q^n = ∅); Observation 1 relates κ^A's pointwise dimensions at each x to the point's effective dimensions. Since κ^A is supported on Q^n with dim^A(p) = 0 for rational p, all its global dimensions are 0.

checks.note: Closed-book answer omits the oracle-relative outer measure kappa^A on Q^n and its four zero global dimensions.

question: Is there a way to handle inductive arguments in a first-order proof system such that normalization still yields analytic proofs — proofs whose formulas all come from the statement being proved?
expected_answer: Standard induction rules weaken the system, and no existing induction-capable system keeps analyticity under normalization. The alternative: schematic proofs that simulate induction by linking proofs together, admitting a normal form of comparable quality; a calculus for constructing them is introduced and shown sound and complete for a fragment of arithmetic.

checks.note: Closed-book answer cites omega-rule which is absent from excerpt.

question: In the experimental evaluation of the progressive trajectory simplification algorithm, which input parameters were varied and which performance metrics were measured, and what alternative implementations were compared?
expected_answer: The experiments varied input length, number of scales, number of shortcuts, and error tolerance, measuring running time and simplification size (cumulative and per scale). They also compared top-down vs bottom-up simplification, and convex hull construction with shortcut intervals against explicit shortcut graph construction, using a single high-granularity trajectory dataset.

question: For the simplified strain gradient elasticity model, what parameters does the strain gradient tensor h depend on, and does it use the same CL, CS and CT coefficients as the elastic tensor?
expected_answer: It depends on E (Young's constant), the Poisson ratio ν, and a single internal length scale l; yes, CL, CS and CT are shared with the elastic tensor and defined in Eq. (71) and (72).

question: In a wireless link whose channel fading h fluctuates during transmission, why does the approximate maximum-likelihood receiver maximize the auxiliary objective L(X, Y) instead of the true log-likelihood ln p(Y), and under what condition does this surrogate become exact?
expected_answer: Because the divergence DKL between the arbitrary q(X) and the true posterior is non-negative, L(X, Y) is a lower bound of ln p(Y), and ln p(Y) is maximized if and only if q(X) = p(X|Y). Since the exact p(Y|X) is problematic as h changes, maximizing L(X, Y) is an effective substitute.

question: In the strongly convex case, what does the proof establish about the change in the inverse optimality gap from one successful iteration to the next, and how is the step size bounded to get there?

This follows because a successful iteration forces αk ≤ 1/(η c3 c), so (1 − η c3 c αk) ∈ [0, 1), giving log(f(x_{k+1}) − f*) ≤ log(1 − η c3 αk) + log(f(x_k) − f*).

question: In the estimation simulation with a circular uniform distribution, do all agents' trajectories of estimates become Lévy walks, or only some agents — and what do the step length distributions of the Min and EMA agents look like?

question: What method is proposed for 3D segmentation of brain arteries and veins when only a small number of labeled scans are available, and which existing natural-image segmentation technique is it built upon?

question: When GRPO is used to RL fine-tune the autoregressive vs. flow-matching policies on LIBERO (starting from a single demonstration per task), which policy trains better and what is the proposed reason for the difference?
expected_answer: The AR policy converges faster, reaches a higher final success rate, and shows lower variance; this is attributed to its native, direct likelihood parameterization that makes policy probability ratios easy to compute, whereas the FM policy needs an SDE-based stochastic approximation of the denoising dynamics, adding optimization sensitivity and gradient variance.

question: In this geometric element detection pipeline for hand–object interaction, how does the system determine which corners, edges, and surface patches on a 3D object can actually be reached by a particular finger?
expected_answer: It computes the finger's movement space by iteratively updating its joint rotations with forward kinematics under joint limits, discards poses where the hand overlaps the object or itself, and treats any geometric elements lying inside that movement space as reachable.

question: When executing the linear blocks of Transformer inference on a 3D flash PIM array, why is the weight matrix split along its columns across planes rather than along its rows, and how are the activation matrices partitioned during prefill versus decode?

question: In this patch-based image classification framework, how is the soft per-patch mask that identifies which patches are relevant for the label prediction computed, and how is it trained?
expected_answer: It is computed from the raw query–key attention scores, averaged over heads and target patches and passed through a sigmoid, giving a soft mask in (0,1)^P. The mask is optimized jointly with the attention parameters under the training objectives, rather than used post-hoc.

question: In the pass@1 results tabulated for code-generation benchmark runs under different probe settings, what do the plus–minus figures appended to each accuracy number represent?

question: In this structured feature tokenization scheme for conversion-rate prediction, how are categorical user ID fields with vocabularies too large for a full embedding table handled, and how does the pipeline keep genuine zero values separate from padding in dense features?

question: In this evaluation, how is the trade-off between prediction accuracy and token cost scored, and what puts a method on the Pareto frontier?
expected_answer: Average final prompt and output tokens per query (upstream operations excluded) are combined with a method's macro-average accuracy over the five benchmarks into a trade-off score; marginal accuracy gain per 1k extra tokens is computed against the zero-shot baseline. Pareto frontiers contain methods for which no displayed method achieves both higher accuracy and lower token use.

question: When transformer depth is grown in curriculum phases by appending new blocks rather than training all layers jointly, does it matter whether normalization is applied to the inputs of each residual branch versus to the residual stream after each update?

question: What AI systems and research areas are in scope for this consensus document on technical AI safety research priorities, and what does it explicitly rule out?
expected_answer: It limits itself to technical AI safety research aimed at making AI more trustworthy rather than more powerful, focusing on general-purpose systems that can perform or be adapted to a wide range of tasks — text-producing language models and multimodal models handling text, images, video, audio, and robotic actions. AI policy research and narrow single-task systems (e.g., autonomous cars) are out of scope.

question: In LLM agentic RL training, when a container in the rollout environment crashes mid-trajectory, how much does the adaptive checkpoint-based recovery slow down rollouts compared with restarting failed trajectories from scratch?

question: In the audio-to-spikes pipeline with a linear SNN classifier, which single encoder hyperparameter has to be tuned when moving to a new audio dataset, and what does tuning it achieve?

question: How can a self-supervised model for music information retrieval combine JEPA-style latent prediction with contrastive learning in a single shared backbone, without needing an EMA teacher?

question: What technique did the descriptive analysis use to group articles into related topics and compare their average scores, and why is that grouping considered only descriptive rather than statistically robust?
expected_answer: k-means clustering (25 clusters) with TF-IDF weighting on titles and abstracts; it is not statistically robust because different clustering methods and their many options produce different outputs.

question: In the Operator Function task, how is the newly defined arithmetic operator constructed, and what factor is expected to determine how hard the task is?
